extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers and experimentalists (late 17th-century scientific readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting small-scale experimental observations and mathematical/methodological treatments in natural philosophy (experiments in chemistry, physiology, hydraulics, and astronomical/mathematical methods for meteorology). Emphasises experimental protocol, specimen comparison, and geometric/arithmetical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact sealing of experimental vessel (no air admitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The glass should be so exactly stopped, that no air be admitted; for an error in one circumstance will mar the whole experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill the phial not much above half and immediately stop it so no air is admitted. A single admission of air will change the course of the experiment; where possible use an air-pump and perform operations in vacuo to preserve states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control filling level and surface area to manage air contact
rubrics_metrics.description: The glass should not be filled much above half; the upper surface becomes first immediately tinged and the tincture penetrates the whole the sooner if the glass be wide, and the liquor consequently have a larger surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrower vessels to slow air-induced changes; pouring the liquid between glasses increases exposure and accelerates colour change. These physical factors are part of experimental control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and report the time-course and reversibility of chemical changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the tincture becoming deeper for 4, 5, or 6 days, then standing 2 or 3 days, afterwards gradually declining until quite pale; upon re-admission of the air, the clear spirit immediately recovers its former blue tincture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record timing of colour deepening, plateau, fading, and immediate restoration on air admission. Decanting the pale spirit away from filings demonstrates that the filings do not re-tint the liquor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decanting and vacuo-preservation as a control to show agent of change
rubrics_metrics.description: When the tincture is pale, decant the clear spirit into a glass leaving the filings behind; if you have an air-pump, pour off in vacuo and stop up close to preserve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decantation proves the colour is not continuously produced by the metal filings. Preservation in vacuo shows that absence of air maintains the pale state; re-admission of air reproduces the original tincture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental analogy to physiological phenomena with structural/functional argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of colour in the experiment is applied to explain changes of colour in the blood of respiring animals: venal blood becomes florid on exposure to air; lungs act as a pneumatic engine effecting the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing physiological conclusions from chemical experiments, cite anatomical structure (e.g., lungs as vesicular pneumatic apparatus), compare observed in vivo colour changes (venous vs arterial), and argue by direct analogy and sequence of observations rather than pure speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification standard for 'volatile salts' (benchmark = water)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard of volatile salts should be settled; at present none better than water. That salt which in distillation is more fixed than water ought not to be reckoned among volatile salts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test volatility by co-distillation with water: if a substance requires a higher degree of heat than water to come over, it is not a volatile salt. Use distilled behaviour relative to water as classificatory criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nitrous salts from true volatile salts (nitre not volatile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nitrous salts seem not to have any property of volatile salt; nitre is a salt of so fixed a nature that it continues melted with scarcely any evaporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not classify nitre or similar fixed salts as volatile; assess chemical behaviour (evaporation/distillation, reactions with alkalies) to place substances in correct category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volatile salts tend to be alkalies and enhance certain tinctures
rubrics_metrics.description: All salts that are truly volatile are really lighter than water and are alkalies; volatile salts are very powerful in extracting tinctures and particularly in heightening those colours disposed to be red.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small proportions of volatile salts to test effects on tinctures (e.g., cochineal, arterial blood). Observe fermentative interactions with other reagents to characterise volatile behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant identification by specimen comparison and literature correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect a dried specimen and compare stalks, leaves and spikes with described species in authoritative works (Ray, Gerard, Bauhin); morphological agreement indicates identity (e.g., dog-mercury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send specimens to botanists/apothecaries for opinion; note ecological/behavioural clues (e.g., cattle never eat it), morphological details (branched, seeded like spinach, dented leaves), and check multiple authors' figures and descriptions to confirm identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report harmful-plant incidents with symptom chronology and post-exposure observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate precise timing: cooking/eating -> 2 hours later onset of sickness -> vomiting/purging -> prolonged sleep; record individual outcomes (recovery, prolonged coma, death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide household context, preparation method, and follow-up by medical authorities; preserve specimen for botanical confirmation and record differing expert opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental protocol for demonstrating hydrostatic pressure via submerged sealed bottle
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop a quart glass bottle with a large cork, tie it down to a rope, sink to bottom and draw up: the cork may be pressed through into the cavity and the bottle be full of seawater; cork soundness determines ingress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sound cork larger than the mouth where possible and tie it; repetition at different depths and with different corks is necessary to show pressure effects; report failures (soaked cork) as evidence of imperfect seal rather than inconsistent pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement and reporting of tidal/periodic phenomena (ebb and flow well)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure amplitude (from high to low water-mark), timing (flux and reflux performed in ~2 minutes, sometimes ~1 minute), count periodic occurrences per hour, and observe bubbles rising at onset of rising water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark a fixed reference, take repeated time measurements, note regularity and repeatability, report sensory properties of the water (taste, mineral impregnation) and local uses (e.g., dietary use in fevers) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical method for computing proportional solar heat (sum of sines approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the simple action of the sun as proportional to the sine of the angle of incidence; erect sines of the sun's altitude as perpendiculars on a time base and the area under the curve is proportional to the collected heat of all the beams in that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce the problem to finding the curved surface of an obliquely cut cylinder, relate figures (analemma projected on meridian) to the cylinder construction, and compute areas via sums/products of sines and semidiurnal arch measures. State assumptions explicitly (simple action proportional to sine; use time of continuance as basis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation recipe for interval solar action (sines × semidiurnal-arch adjustments)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given interval, multiply the sum of the sines of the meridian altitudes by half the sum (or half the difference) of the sines of the horary distances; in summer add (in winter subtract) the product of half the arch corresponding to the interval into the difference of the sines of meridian altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Van Ceulen's numbers for arch measures; perform arithmetic carefully (examples and worked table provided); compute for representative latitudes (tables for every 10th degree) to estimate intermediate degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: State corollaries and proportional relationships for comparing heats
rubrics_metrics.description: Several notable corollaries: (1) equinoctial heat when sun vertical is as twice the square of radius (a standard); (2) under the equinoctial the heat is as the sine of the sun's declination; (3) in frigid zones when sun does not set, heat is as circumference×sine of altitude at 6; (4) equinoctial day's heat is everywhere as the cosine of the latitude; (5) differences between summer and winter heats are as sines of latitude×sines of declination; (6) tropical sun under equinoctial has least force; polar day may exceed equinoctial by 5:4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these proportionalities as standards for comparing solar action across latitudes and declinations; apply the tabulated computed values to form general ideas of yearly aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-edition appraisal criteria (fidelity, accuracy, elegancy, perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: An edition may be assessed for fidelity, accuracy, elegancy, and perfection in all points (printing / editorial quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing editions, compare against former editions and judge improvements in fidelity to source, editorial accuracy, typographical elegance, and overall perfection of the production.
